person.name: Vannevar_Bush
person.summary: Vannevar Bush was an American engineer and science administrator who organized much of the United States' wartime research during World War II. He built influential analog computers, proposed the memex, and pressed the federal government to sustain basic scientific research.

conclusion: Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer helped establish the use of analog machines for scientific and engineering calculation. His essay As We May Think informed later work on hypertext, personal computing, and digital information systems. The National Science Foundation funds research and education across American universities, laboratories, and scientific organizations.

events.title: Birth in Everett
events.description: Vannevar Bush was born in Everett, Massachusetts, to Richard Perry Bush, a local [[Universalist pastor]], and Emma Linwood Paine Bush. He was the third child and only son in a family that included his older sisters, Edith and Reba.

Universalist pastor.explanation: A Universalist pastor was a minister in a Christian tradition that taught universal salvation. Richard Perry Bush served the local congregation in Everett.

events.title: Graduates from Tufts
events.description: Vannevar Bush graduated from Tufts College in Medford, Massachusetts, in 1913. Tufts awarded him Bachelor of Science and Master of Science degrees. For his master’s thesis, he designed and patented a [[profile tracer]], a wheeled device that helped surveyors plot terrain.

profile tracer.explanation: Bush’s profile tracer recorded the contours of ground as it moved over terrain. It was his first patented invention.

events.title: Earns Engineering Doctorate
events.description: In April 1916, Vannevar Bush submitted a doctoral thesis on oscillating-current circuits at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts. MIT and Harvard University awarded him a joint doctorate in engineering. His MIT adviser, Arthur Edwin Kennelly, demanded additional work. The department chairman overruled Kennelly after Bush refused, while Bush sought the financial security to marry Phoebe Clara Davis.

images.caption: Massachusetts Institute of Technology campus, circa 1916
images.creator: Detroit Publishing Company

events.background:
A $1,500 scholarship had brought Bush to Clark University for doctoral study under Arthur Gordon Webster. Webster wanted him to work in acoustics. Bush left rather than take up a subject that did not interest him, then entered MIT's electrical engineering program.

The submitted dissertation carried the full title Oscillating-Current Circuits: An Extension of the Theory of Generalized Angular Velocities, with Applications to the Coupled Circuit and the Artificial Transmission Line. Its subject joined mathematical theory to coupled electrical circuits and artificial transmission lines.

background_images.caption: Schematic of an artificial telephone line section for 6000 feet of 24 gauge twisted pair.
background_images.creator: Constant314

events.title: Marries Phoebe Davis
events.description: In August 1916, Vannevar Bush married Phoebe Clara Davis. They had dated while both lived in Chelsea, Massachusetts. Bush taught at Tufts College and worked in electrical engineering as their married life began.

events.title: Joins MIT Faculty
events.description: In 1919, Vannevar Bush left Tufts University for the Department of Electrical Engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He worked under department head Dugald C. Jackson. He also continued work with [[AMRAD|the American Radio and Research Corporation]], a radio company connected to his earlier work at Tufts.

AMRAD.explanation: The American Radio and Research Corporation was a radio company whose laboratory Bush continued to work for after leaving Tufts. It had begun broadcasting music from the Tufts campus in 1916.

events.title: Launches Electronics Venture
events.description: On July 7, 1922, Laurence K. Marshall established the American Appliance Company with Vannevar Bush, Richard S. Aldrich, and Charles G. Smith as directors. The company first pursued silent refrigerators. It later made electronic devices, including Smith’s [[S-tube]] voltage regulator.

S-tube.explanation: The S-tube was a voltage-regulator tube developed by Charles G. Smith. It allowed radios to operate from household electrical power instead of requiring two different types of batteries.

events.title: Builds Differential Analyzer
events.description: At MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Vannevar Bush began building the differential analyzer, a mechanical analog computer for solving differential equations, in 1927. He built on an integraph, a machine that performed graphical integration, made earlier by Herbert R. Stewart. Harold Hazen proposed extending Stewart’s work to second-order differential equations. Bush supervised Hazen as the analyzer was completed in 1931.

images.caption: Vannevar Bush working on the product integraph
images.creator: George H. Davis, Jr. (1126 Boylston St, Boston). Published in the Tech Review

event_class.title: Differential Analyzer
event_class.description: A mechanical and electrical analog computer uses interconnected integrators, shafts, and pens to calculate and plot solutions to differential equations.
event_class.impact: The analyzer became a model for later analog computers used in scientific and engineering calculation.

events.background:
The machine’s six integrators could be linked with an epicyclic differential mechanism that added or subtracted their outputs. Gear ratios set whole-number multiplication or division. Fractional settings required an operator to keep a stylus on a multiplier table. The same table could also represent functions such as polynomials.

Bush called the device a “continuous integraph” in a 1928 article. His 1931 article gave it the name “differential analyzer.” He wrote that its interconnected integrators shared a basic idea with Lord Kelvin’s earlier design. Bush later said that he had learned of Kelvin’s work only after the first machine was operating. The Franklin Institute awarded him the Louis E. Levy Medal in 1928.

Claude Shannon ran the analyzer in Bush’s laboratory in 1936. Its complicated circuits led Shannon to develop switching circuits based on Boolean algebra for his 1937 master’s thesis.

background_images.caption: Exhibit in the MIT Museum - Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA. As a useful object, this work is not subject to copyright protection.
background_images.creator: Daderot

events.title: Leads MIT Engineering
events.description: In 1932, MIT president Karl T. Compton appointed Vannevar Bush vice president of the institute and dean of its School of Engineering in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Bush continued his engineering research and industry work while holding the two offices.

images.caption: Karl Compton meets with Vannevar Bush in 1932
images.creator: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Historical Collections, courtesy AIP Emilio Segrè Visual Archives

events.title: Takes Carnegie Presidency
events.description: In May 1938, Vannevar Bush accepted the presidency of the Carnegie Institution of Washington in Washington, D.C. The privately endowed research institution operated eight major laboratories. Its annual research budget was about $1.5 million.

images.caption: Carnegie Institution administration building in Washington
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author

events.title: Organizes Defense Research
events.description: President Franklin D. Roosevelt approved Vannevar Bush’s proposal for the [[National Defense Research Committee|National Defense Research Committee (NDRC)]] on June 12, 1940. The committee was formally established on June 27 with Bush as chairman. Bush brought university scientists, industrial researchers, and military representatives together to coordinate defense research.

images.caption: First meeting of the National Defense Research Committee
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author

National Defense Research Committee.explanation: The National Defense Research Committee was a federal organization created to coordinate scientific research for military purposes during World War II. It operated under Bush’s leadership until its work was incorporated into the Office of Scientific Research and Development in 1941.

events.title: Directs OSRD
events.description: On June 28, 1941, President Franklin D. Roosevelt established the Office of Scientific Research and Development by Executive Order 8807. He appointed Vannevar Bush to direct the civilian agency. The OSRD absorbed the National Defense Research Committee and coordinated military, medical, and scientific research for the United States war effort.
events.background:
Congressional appropriations gave the new office the money to operate on a far larger scale. It grew to 850 full-time employees, handled roughly 2,500 contracts worth over $536 million, and generated between 30,000 and 35,000 reports. Its work included medical research and the mass production of penicillin and sulfa drugs.

Bush set broad policy and left individual divisions to qualified supervisors. He kept the agency's mission narrowly defined to prevent duplicated work across government offices. Funding decisions required him to divide projects among government laboratories, universities, and industry. Military leaders questioned whether civilian researchers could keep secrets and deliver usable equipment. The struggle to retain scientific workers sharpened during the Army's 1944 manpower crisis. The OSRD requested draft deferments for about 9,725 employees of its contractors. All but 63 were approved.

events.title: Guides Atomic Bomb Program
events.description: In 1942, Vannevar Bush pressed for the American atomic-bomb program to move under Army control. He sought faster construction and clearer oversight. Bush chaired the Military Policy Committee with James B. Conant, Brigadier General Wilhelm D. Styer, and Rear Admiral William R. Purnell. The committee supervised the program under President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Top Policy Group.

images.caption: Vannevar Bush with American commanders, circa 1944
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author

Manhattan Project.explanation: The Manhattan Project was the United States Army-led program to develop atomic weapons during World War II. In 1942, its administration was reorganized and accelerated under Army direction.

events.title: Publishes As We May Think
events.description: In July 1945, Vannevar Bush published As We May Think, reworking ideas from his 1939 essay Mechanization and the Record. He called for better access to accumulated scientific knowledge. He described the [[memex]], a hypothetical microfilm system for storing documents and notes. Its users could create [[associative trails|linked sequences of documents and annotations]].

images.caption: Illustration from Vannevar Bush's As We May Think
images.creator: Time Inc.

associative trails.explanation: An associative trail was Bush’s proposed way to connect an arbitrary sequence of microfilm pages with links, comments, and side paths. Users could save and share these trails as organized routes through information.

memex.explanation: The memex was Bush’s proposed personal information machine. It used microfilm and controls to let a user store, retrieve, and connect records.

event_class.title: As We May Think
event_class.impact: The essay influenced later developers of hypertext, personal computing, and systems for organizing digital information.

events.background:
The essay came out as Bush worried about science’s destructive wartime uses. He urged scientists to improve access to the accumulated record of human knowledge. He objected to alphabetical and numerical filing systems that forced a record into a single location unless it was copied. He argued that machines could take over tedious numerical tasks and leave people to work on scientific theory.

Bush grounded the proposal in technologies he considered attainable. He envisioned ultra-high-resolution microfilm, cameras, several viewing screens, and electromechanical controls built into a desk-sized private library. Electric photocells would read coded symbols beside microfilm frames while reels ran at high speed and stopped on command. A transparent platen would let a user photograph handwritten notes, photographs, and memoranda onto blank spaces on the machine’s film.

A September 10 abridgment in Life carried fanciful illustrations of the desk and related devices. Alfred D. Crimi’s illustration pictured a desk that could bring files and materials rapidly to its operator.

events.title: Presents a Postwar Science Plan
events.description: On July 25, 1945, Vannevar Bush delivered Science, The Endless Frontier to President Harry S. Truman in Washington, D.C. The report called for sustained federal support for basic research. It also called for investment in medical research, scientific education, and civilian uses of wartime discoveries.

event_class.title: Science, The Endless Frontier
event_class.impact: The report supplied a framework for expanded federal support of scientific research after World War II.

events.title: Congress Creates the National Science Foundation
events.description: On May 10, 1950, President Harry S. Truman signed legislation creating the National Science Foundation (NSF). The law established a federal agency to support civilian scientific research, a goal Vannevar Bush had advocated in his 1945 report Science, the Endless Frontier.

events.title: Leaves Carnegie Institution
events.description: In 1955, Vannevar Bush ended his presidency of the Carnegie Institution of Washington. He had led the institution since 1938.

events.title: Death in Belmont
events.description: Vannevar Bush died in Belmont, Massachusetts, on June 28, 1974, after a [[stroke]]. His wife, Phoebe Clara Davis Bush, had died in 1969. Bush spent his final years near Boston.

stroke.explanation: A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel in the brain ruptures. It can cause sudden and severe impairment or death.
